subtopic_detail: Bedwetting five nights a week in a seven year old who has never been reliably dry overnight
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a seven year old boy and his mother about bedwetting. He wets on about five nights a week and has never had more than three consecutive dry nights.

He has no daytime wetting, no urgency and no straining, and he opens his bowels daily with soft stools. He drinks most of his fluid after school because he does not like the school toilets. He is otherwise well, growing along the fiftieth centile and doing well at school, and he has recently started refusing sleepovers with his cousins. Examination of his abdomen, spine, lower limb neurology and external genitalia is normal, and his urine dipstick shows no glucose, protein, blood, nitrites or leucocytes. His mother is willing to be woken at night and the family is committed to a treatment plan.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable faecal loading, normal lumbosacral spine with no sacral dimple or hair tuft, normal lower limb tone power and reflexes, normal external genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for glucose, protein, blood, nitrites and leucocytes; bladder diary shows normal daytime voiding frequency and volumes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe desmopressin each night and continue it until he has been dry for three consecutive months
options.rationale: Desmopressin works while it is being taken but relapse after cessation is common, so it is chosen for short term cover such as a camp or when an alarm has failed or cannot be used. It also carries a hyponatraemia risk requiring evening fluid restriction (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

options.text: Start oxybutynin at night to increase his functional bladder capacity while he is asleep
options.rationale: Anticholinergic therapy targets overactive bladder, which typically produces daytime urgency and frequency that he does not have. It is added for children with proven detrusor overactivity resistant to first line measures (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

options.text: Arrange an enuresis alarm program with structured family support and review after several weeks
options.rationale: The alarm is first line for monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a school aged child, with the highest sustained dry rate because it produces conditioned waking rather than temporary symptom suppression. Success requires a motivated family who will wake with the child, which is present here (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

options.text: Advise that he drinks nothing after four in the afternoon and reassess the pattern in three months
options.rationale: Restricting evening fluid without addressing his poor daytime intake reduces total intake and shrinks functional bladder capacity, making matters worse. Redistributing fluid across the school day is helpful, but as an adjunct rather than a treatment (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

options.text: Refer him to a paediatric urologist for renal tract ultrasound and urodynamic assessment first
options.rationale: Imaging and urodynamics are reserved for daytime symptoms, abnormal urinary stream, neurological signs or treatment failure, none of which apply to uncomplicated night time wetting. Referral first delays a treatment that most families can start immediately (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

explanation.summary: Nocturnal enuresis is described as monosymptomatic when there are no daytime urinary symptoms, and it affects a substantial minority of children at school entry with spontaneous resolution at roughly 15 per cent per year. Assessment focuses on excluding daytime symptoms, constipation, an abnormal stream, neurological signs, and the polyuria of diabetes, all of which change the pathway. Constipation is the most commonly missed contributor and treating it alone resolves wetting in many children. Alarm therapy has the best sustained outcomes and works by conditioning arousal to bladder fullness, but requires a committed family and typically several weeks before dryness is achieved. Desmopressin gives faster symptomatic control and is useful for short term needs, while combination therapy is used when either alone is insufficient.
key_points: Monosymptomatic enuresis has no daytime urinary symptoms and needs no imaging
Exclude and treat constipation before starting specific therapy
The alarm is first line with the highest sustained dry rate but takes weeks and requires family commitment
Desmopressin gives rapid short term cover and relapses commonly on cessation
Evening fluid restriction without daytime redistribution reduces functional bladder capacity
explanation.pearls: Continue an alarm until the child achieves fourteen consecutive dry nights before stopping, because ceasing at the first run of dry nights is a leading cause of relapse.

subtopic_detail: Immunisation planning for a well four year old newly arrived in Australia with no written vaccination records
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a four year old girl who arrived in Australia six weeks ago with her family after two years in a refugee camp. She is being enrolled in kindergarten next month.

Her mother believes she received some injections as a baby but has no documentation and no way of contacting the clinic that gave them. The child is thriving, has had no serious illness and takes no medication, and she has never had an allergic reaction to a vaccine or to egg. Her examination is normal and her growth is on the twenty fifth centile for height and weight. Her mother is anxious that the child should not receive injections she has already had.

data_table.Examination: Well grown and thriving, no chronic illness, no immunosuppression, no scars suggestive of previous vaccination, no allergies
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination normal, no immunisation record available on the Australian Immunisation Register

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to her immunisation?

options.text: Wait until documentary evidence of her previous vaccinations can be obtained from her country of origin
options.rationale: Records are frequently unobtainable and waiting leaves a susceptible child unprotected while she enters group care. Documentation is used when it is available and reliable, but its absence must not delay the schedule (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Perform serology for every vaccine preventable disease and immunise only against those she lacks
options.rationale: Serology is not available or interpretable for all antigens, delays protection and is more expensive and distressing than vaccinating. It has a defined role for a few conditions such as hepatitis B and varicella in older children rather than as a blanket strategy (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Give one vaccine at each visit at monthly intervals to minimise the chance of an adverse reaction
options.rationale: Multiple vaccines can be safely administered at the same visit at separate sites, and spacing them out prolongs susceptibility and increases the chance the schedule is never completed. Separation is required only for specific live vaccine timing rules (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Treat her as unvaccinated and begin an age appropriate catch up schedule at today's visit
options.rationale: A child without written documentation is presumed unvaccinated and started on a catch up schedule determined by age, because repeating doses already received is safe while leaving gaps is not. Doses are recorded on the Australian Immunisation Register, which also underpins her family assistance and childcare enrolment requirements (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).
source_refs: Department of Health: Catch up immunisation calculator

options.text: Give only the vaccines required for kindergarten entry now and complete the remainder after she settles
options.rationale: A partial schedule leaves her unprotected against diseases with significant morbidity and relies on a return visit that often does not happen in newly arrived families. Entry requirements set a minimum administrative standard rather than a clinical target (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

explanation.summary: Newly arrived refugee and migrant children frequently have absent or unreliable immunisation records, and the Australian Immunisation Handbook directs that any dose without written documentation be considered not given. Repeat doses of routine childhood vaccines in an already immune child carry no additional risk beyond local reactions, whereas assuming protection that does not exist has serious consequences. Catch up schedules are calculated by age using the online calculator, with minimum intervals between doses rather than the routine intervals, and multiple vaccines are given at the same visit at separate sites. Refugee health assessment also includes screening for tuberculosis, hepatitis B, human immunodeficiency virus, strongyloides, schistosomiasis where relevant, and iron and vitamin D deficiency. All doses are recorded on the Australian Immunisation Register, which matters for childcare enrolment and family payments.
key_points: Undocumented doses are treated as not given and a full catch up schedule is started
Repeat doses of routine childhood vaccines are safe in an already immune child
Multiple vaccines may be given at the same visit at separate injection sites
Catch up schedules use minimum rather than routine intervals and are calculated by age
Serology has a limited targeted role rather than a blanket one
explanation.pearls: Use the national catch up calculator rather than the routine schedule, because it applies the shortened minimum intervals that let a child complete a multi dose course in weeks instead of months.

sources.label: Department of Health: Catch up immunisation calculator

subtopic_detail: Short stature with absent pubertal signs in a fourteen year old boy whose bone age is markedly delayed
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 14 year old boy whose parents are worried he is the smallest in his year. He is 149 cm tall, sitting on the third centile, and weighs 40 kg.

Serial measurements from his school show he has grown 4.5 cm in each of the past two years, tracking parallel to but below the third centile line. He has no headaches, no visual disturbance, no vomiting, no abdominal symptoms and normal energy. He plays cricket and says the height difference does not bother him much, though his parents disagree. His father did not shave until he was nineteen and grew after leaving school. On examination his testicular volume is 3 mL bilaterally with no pubic hair, his visual fields are full, and his fundi are normal. His bone age is reported as eleven years and six months.

data_table.Examination: Height 149 cm on the third centile, weight 40 kg, mid parental target height on the twenty fifth centile, testicular volume 3 mL bilaterally, Tanner stage 1 pubic hair, full visual fields, normal fundi
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination, electrolytes, coeliac serology, thyroid function and insulin like growth factor 1 all within normal limits for bone age, bone age 11 years 6 months at a chronological age of 14 years 2 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence growth hormone therapy and monitor his growth velocity every three months on treatment
options.rationale: Growth hormone is indicated for proven deficiency or for specific conditions on defined criteria, and his normal insulin like growth factor 1 with a preserved growth velocity argues against deficiency. Treating a normal variant exposes him to injections and cost for no gain in final height (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary to exclude an intracranial cause of his delay
options.rationale: Imaging is prompted by headache, visual field loss, growth velocity failure, diabetes insipidus or a discordant clinical picture, none of which is present. His normal fields, fundi and preserved velocity make an intracranial lesion very unlikely (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

options.text: Request a karyotype and gonadotropin levels to investigate a possible chromosomal cause of short stature
options.rationale: Karyotyping is indicated for dysmorphic features, disproportionate stature or a girl with unexplained short stature, and gonadotropins are hard to interpret before the pubertal window has passed. A family history of delayed puberty with delayed bone age points elsewhere (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

options.text: Give a three month course of low dose testosterone to accelerate his growth and pubertal development
options.rationale: A short androgen course is a legitimate option when delay is causing significant psychological distress, which he does not report, and it advances puberty without increasing final height. It is offered after discussion rather than as routine management of a normal variant (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

options.text: Explain the pattern to the family and review his height and pubertal staging every six months
options.rationale: A normal growth velocity tracking parallel to the centiles, a bone age delayed by more than two years, prepubertal testicular volume at 14 and a family history of late puberty describe constitutional delay of growth and puberty, which reaches a normal adult height without treatment. Regular review confirms the expected pubertal progression and detects the minority whose velocity falters (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

explanation.summary: Short stature is assessed by plotting serial heights, calculating growth velocity, comparing with the mid parental target range and obtaining a bone age, since the pattern over time discriminates far better than any single measurement. Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is the commonest cause of a short prepubertal adolescent boy, characterised by a delayed bone age, a normal growth velocity, a positive family history and eventual attainment of a height within the target range. Growth failure, defined by crossing centiles downward or a velocity below the expected range, points instead to pathology such as hypothyroidism, coeliac disease, growth hormone deficiency, chronic illness or an intracranial lesion. Basic screening includes full blood examination, renal and liver function, thyroid function, coeliac serology and insulin like growth factor 1. Psychological impact is asked about explicitly because it, rather than the height itself, most often drives the decision to intervene.
key_points: Growth velocity and bone age matter more than a single height measurement
Delayed bone age with normal velocity and a family history indicates constitutional delay
Crossing centiles downward signals pathology and prompts investigation
Growth hormone is for proven deficiency or specific defined indications
A short androgen course is reserved for significant psychological distress
explanation.pearls: A bone age delayed by more than two years alongside a normal growth velocity predicts a final height within the mid parental target range, which is the specific reassurance families need rather than a general statement that he will catch up.

subtopic_detail: Imaging decisions after a first febrile urinary tract infection that responded promptly in an eight month old
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an eight month old girl in the clinic ten days after she completed treatment for her first urinary tract infection. She had presented with three days of fever to 39.2 degrees C, vomiting and irritability with no localising signs.

A catheter specimen grew Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole, and she was afebrile and feeding normally within 30 hours of starting oral antibiotics. Her antenatal ultrasound scans were normal and there is no family history of renal disease or vesicoureteric reflux. Today she is well, thriving on the fiftieth centile, has a normal abdominal examination with no palpable bladder or kidneys, and a good urinary stream reported by her mother. Her blood pressure is normal for age and her creatinine measured during the admission was normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128 per minute, blood pressure 88/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Catheter urine culture grew Escherichia coli greater than 10^8 colony forming units per litre, sensitive to trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole; creatinine normal for age; antenatal ultrasound scans reported as normal
data_table.Examination: Thriving on the fiftieth centile, abdomen soft with no palpable bladder or kidneys, normal external genitalia, normal spine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: Arrange no routine imaging and advise prompt urine testing with any future unexplained fever
options.rationale: A first urinary tract infection in an infant over six months that is caused by Escherichia coli and responds within 48 hours is a typical infection, for which routine imaging is not required in Australian paediatric guidance. The family instead receives clear advice to seek early urine testing with future febrile illness, since recurrence is the trigger for imaging (Source: RCH Melbourne: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Request a renal tract ultrasound now to exclude an underlying structural abnormality of the kidneys
options.rationale: Ultrasound is recommended for infants under six months with a first infection, for atypical infections and for recurrent infections, none of which describes her. Ordering it in a typical infection yields little and generates incidental findings and further tests (Source: RCH Melbourne: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Organise a dimercaptosuccinic acid scan in four to six months to look for evidence of renal scarring
options.rationale: Cortical scintigraphy is reserved for children with recurrent or atypical infection, or where an abnormal ultrasound raises concern about scarring. Performing it after a single typical infection exposes a well infant to radiation without changing management (Source: RCH Melbourne: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Refer her for a micturating cystourethrogram to determine whether vesicoureteric reflux is present
options.rationale: This invasive study is used for atypical or recurrent infection, an abnormal ultrasound, or a strong family history of reflux, and it requires catheterisation with radiation exposure. Identifying low grade reflux after a single typical infection does not alter outcomes (Source: RCH Melbourne: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Commence nightly antibiotic prophylaxis and continue it until she reaches her second birthday
options.rationale: Prophylaxis after a single typical infection provides minimal reduction in recurrence and selects resistant organisms, and it is considered only for high grade reflux or frequent recurrences. Prompt treatment of recurrences protects the kidney better than continuous low dose therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Australian practice has moved away from imaging every child after a first urinary tract infection, because most abnormalities detected do not alter management and investigation carries radiation, catheterisation and incidental finding costs. An infection is classified as atypical when the child is seriously ill or septic, has poor urine flow, an abdominal or bladder mass, raised creatinine, a non Escherichia coli organism, or fails to respond within 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics. Ultrasound is recommended for infants under six months with a first infection, for any atypical infection and for recurrent infection, with cortical scintigraphy and cystourethrography reserved for narrower indications. The most valuable intervention for a well infant after a typical infection is family education about testing urine early during future febrile illness. Age under three months, systemic toxicity or inability to tolerate oral therapy remain indications for intravenous treatment at the time of infection.
key_points: Typical infection means Escherichia coli with a response within 48 hours in a child who is not septic
Ultrasound is indicated under six months of age, for atypical infections and for recurrent infections
Cortical scintigraphy and cystourethrography have narrower recurrent or atypical indications
Prophylaxis is not routine after a single typical infection
Early urine testing during future febrile illness is the highest yield family advice
explanation.pearls: Collect the specimen by catheter or suprapubic aspirate in a non toilet trained child, since bag specimens have a false positive rate high enough that a positive bag culture should never be used to diagnose infection or to trigger imaging.

subtopic_detail: Sudden severe scrotal pain overnight in an adolescent with an absent cremasteric reflex
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 14 year old boy who woke at two in the morning with severe left scrotal pain and has vomited twice. It is now five hours since the pain began and he is pale and reluctant to walk.

He has had no dysuria, no urethral discharge, no fever and no recent trauma, and he is not sexually active. He describes a similar but briefer episode three months ago that settled after twenty minutes. The left hemiscrotum is swollen and exquisitely tender with the testis sitting higher than the right and lying transversely. There is no cremasteric reflex on the left and elevating the testis does not relieve his pain. His urine dipstick is negative for nitrites and leucocytes. The on call surgical team is in the hospital and theatre is available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Left testis high riding and transverse, exquisitely tender, absent left cremasteric reflex, no relief on elevation, right testis normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for nitrites, leucocytes and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange an urgent scrotal ultrasound with Doppler and act on the findings when they are available
options.rationale: Imaging in a case with this clinical picture only delays surgery and can be falsely reassuring in early or intermittent torsion where flow is preserved. Ultrasound is helpful when the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain and would not otherwise lead to exploration (Source: RCH Melbourne: Acute scrotal pain).

options.text: Refer him for immediate surgical exploration of the scrotum with bilateral fixation as indicated
options.rationale: Sudden severe pain with vomiting, a high riding transverse testis and an absent cremasteric reflex is torsion until proven otherwise, and salvage falls sharply after about six hours of ischaemia. Exploration allows detorsion with fixation of both testes, since the anatomical predisposition is usually bilateral (Source: RCH Melbourne: Acute scrotal pain).

options.text: Start oral antibiotics for epididymo orchitis and review him in the clinic within 48 hours
options.rationale: Epididymo orchitis is rare in a prepubertal or non sexually active adolescent, develops over days with dysuria or pyuria, and is typically relieved by elevating the testis. His negative dipstick and sudden onset point away from infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give strong analgesia and reassess him in the morning when the surgical clinic list is running
options.rationale: Any delay of hours in a testis that has already been ischaemic for five hours converts a salvageable organ into an infarcted one. Analgesia is given while theatre is prepared, never as a reason to wait (Source: RCH Melbourne: Acute scrotal pain).

options.text: Send a first pass urine sample for nucleic acid testing and treat according to the result obtained
options.rationale: Sexually transmitted infection testing is appropriate for a sexually active young man with a subacute painful epididymis, not for this presentation. Waiting for a result would waste the remaining window for testicular salvage (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a time critical diagnosis with two incidence peaks, in the neonatal period and around puberty, and salvage rates fall from above 90 per cent within six hours to well under half beyond twelve. The classic features are abrupt severe pain often waking the patient from sleep, nausea and vomiting, a high riding transversely lying testis and an absent cremasteric reflex, and a history of prior self limiting episodes suggests intermittent torsion. Doppler ultrasound is useful when the picture is equivocal but must never delay exploration when the clinical suspicion is high, since preserved arterial flow can be seen in partial or early torsion. The main differentials are torsion of the appendix testis, which produces a localised upper pole tenderness with a blue dot sign, and epididymo orchitis, which develops over days with urinary symptoms. Fixation is performed bilaterally because the underlying bell clapper anatomy is usually present on both sides.
key_points: Abrupt pain with vomiting, a high riding transverse testis and absent cremasteric reflex indicates torsion
Salvage rates fall sharply beyond six hours of symptom onset
Doppler flow may be preserved in partial or intermittent torsion, so imaging must not delay theatre
Prior brief self limiting episodes suggest intermittent torsion and support urgent exploration
Both testes are fixed at operation because the predisposing anatomy is usually bilateral
explanation.pearls: Manual detorsion by rotating the testis outward like opening a book can restore flow while theatre is prepared, but it relieves pain in only some patients and never replaces exploration with fixation.
